title: Quitting ultra-processed food may ease depression, small UCSF study finds
excerpt: In a first-of-its-kind 20-person crossover trial published in JAMA Psychiatry, participants who cut ultra-processed food by 85% saw moderate-to-large improvements in depression symptoms.
body:
• Twenty adults with depression cut ultra-processed food intake by more than 85% and showed moderate-to-large improvements across three depression measures.
  • The UCSF pilot, published September 23, 2026 in JAMA Psychiatry, is believed to be the first to compare the same participants' symptoms before and after a diet switch.
  • All participants had a high BMI and at least one metabolic disorder; 14 also had anxiety, which improved modestly.
  • The findings are preliminary: enrollment for a larger phase 2 trial is expected to begin in 2028.

What the study found

Cutting ultra-processed food from the diet may help ease symptoms of depression, according to a small but first-of-its-kind pilot study from the University of California, San Francisco, published September 23 in JAMA Psychiatry.

The trial enrolled 20 adults aged 18 to 80 with a primary diagnosis of depression, a Patient Health Questionnaire-9 score of at least 5, and diets heavy in ultra-processed food: they scored in the top third on a screening questionnaire of highly processed food consumption, averaging 10.10 on the scale. In an open-label, order-randomized crossover design, participants spent four weeks on their usual diet and four weeks on a low-ultra-processed diet, choosing and buying their own food with guidance from the research team. Nineteen participants completed the study.

By the end of the low-ultra-processed period, participants had cut their intake of such foods by more than 85% — the average screening score fell to 1.42. Compared with their usual-diet weeks, they recorded moderate-to-large improvements across three different measures of depression. Anxiety, which affected 14 of the participants, also improved modestly.

"Junky processing may harm your gut in ways that ripple up to your brain."

— Dr. Nyasha Chagwedera, corresponding author, UCSF Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences

Context & Background

Ultra-processed foods — packaged snacks, fast food, sugary drinks and other industrially manufactured products — typically contain preservatives, artificial coloring, flavor enhancers and emulsifiers. They make up a large share of calories in many modern diets, and observational studies have linked heavy consumption to depression. This study, funded by the National Institutes of Health, is believed to be the first to measure depression symptoms in the same people before and after a deliberate shift away from such foods.

The study population was medically complex: average age 44, 70% female, all with a high body-mass index and at least one metabolic disorder such as hypertension, diabetes or elevated LDL cholesterol. "Reducing the amount of ultra-processed food in our diet can be challenging, because it's highly palatable, cheap, and convenient," Chagwedera said. "Ultra-processed food triggers dopamine, the pleasure hormone, which promotes craving. Food companies work with scientists to find just the right amount of sugar, salt, and fat that make you want to eat more and more."

Impact & Analysis

The crossover design is the study's real strength: because each participant served as their own control, the improvements can't easily be dismissed as differences between healthier and less healthy people. Participants also rated the diet feasible and acceptable, scoring its ease and utility above 5 on a 7-point scale.

Chagwedera, who founded the UCSF Metabolic and Mental Health Program, points to the gut-brain axis as the likely mechanism: ultra-processed foods may damage the protective lining of the gut, creating what she described as a "leaky, out-of-balance gut" that drives low-grade, chronic inflammation — which either directly causes depression or makes people more vulnerable to it.

The caveats are real. Twenty participants is tiny, the trial was open-label, and the effect could shrink in a larger, blinded study. Senior author Dr. Andrew Krystal framed the work accordingly, saying it "successfully established the viability of carrying out this research in a larger-scale trial." This is a green light for bigger research, not a prescription.

Diaspora Angle

For South Asian diaspora households, the findings land in a familiar kitchen tension: long work hours make frozen ready meals and packaged snacks the default, while traditional home cooking — dal, sabzi, roti, fermented foods — already resembles the minimally processed pattern the study tested. None of this is medical advice, but the research gives one more reason to treat everyday home cooking as health infrastructure rather than nostalgia.

What's Next

The researchers plan a larger depression trial, with enrollment for phase 2 expected to begin in 2028. Until then, guidelines are unlikely to change on the basis of 20 people — but the gut-brain connection has one more data point, and it points away from the snack aisle.
